Blender add-on · garment simulation

Clothing Design

Draw flat pattern pieces, sew them together, and simulate them onto your character — the pattern-cutter's way of working, built natively on Blender's cloth solver.

Watch it work

Start to finish: measuring the body, drafting the flat pieces, wrapping them on, stitching the seams closed, welding, settling, pulling the cloth about with the grab tool — then the same pipeline run for a tank top, a skirt and trousers.

The workspace

The Clothing Design tab is added to every file you open. It is a real Blender workspace: a 2D pattern view, a side elevation, the 3D garment view with the Clothing sidebar, physics properties, outliner and timeline.

Workflow

Six steps, in order. Everything lives in the Clothing sidebar (N) of the 3D view.

  1. 01
    Import Default Character

    Brings in the bundled fitting avatar and measures it. Sets the collider in the same step.

    Panel: Avatar

  2. 02
    Add Garment Draw Pattern

    Pick a preset, or click your own outline in the 2D view — Enter closes the shape. Every click run becomes a named edge you can sew.

    Panel: Patterns

  3. 03
    Counterpart

    Copies the selected piece to the opposite side of the body and sews the edges that meet. This is the “draw the front, get the back” step.

    Panel: Patterns

  4. 04
    Arrange on Body Auto Sew

    Rebuilds the 3D garment from the flat pieces. With Live Sync on, any change to a piece’s height, spin, wrap or ease re-arranges it immediately.

    Panels: Patterns, Seams

  5. 05
    Sew & Drape

    Runs the three phases: stitch at low gravity, weld the closed seams, settle at full gravity.

    Panel: Simulate

  6. 06
    Finalize Garment

    Freezes the draped shape, adds thickness, transfers skin weights from the body and binds to the rig, so the garment follows your animation.

    Panel: Finalize

The fitting avatar

The bundled character is the project model with no clothing, a neutral face and the feet flattened onto the floor. The original is posed for high heels — it still carries a hidden High_Heels object and a 44 mm sole tilt in its rest pose. Each ankle angle was solved numerically (15.6° left, 14.4° right) and the body dropped so it stands at exactly z = 0.

From flat pattern to garment

Drafting is solved, not guessed

Each preset derives its shape from the body rather than from fixed proportions:

  • The neckline half‑width is solved so the finished opening measures 1.12× the true neck girth — measured at the narrowest slice above the shoulders, not at the neck base, which includes the trapezius and is far too big.
  • The armhole depth is solved so the armhole measures 1.3× the biceps.
  • The sleeve cap width is then found by bisection so the cap curve matches the armhole it is sewn to — 45.0 cm of cap against a 44.2 cm armhole. A cap longer than its armhole is exactly what gathers a sleeve into a crumpled mess.

Quad cage, subdivided surface

Pattern pieces are built as a quad grid clipped to the outline, not a triangulation. A quad cage subdivides into a clean surface, and its edges run along the pattern’s own axes, so the cloth stretches along the grain the way woven fabric does. Panels come out 100% quads at about 85° minimum corner angle.

LevelRendered facesFold angleDrape
0 — cage2,29019.4°8 s
1 — default8,8928.4°8 s
235,0324.4°15 s
Order matters. Modifiers are held in Armature → Cloth → Subdivision → Solidify. With the subdivision ahead of the cloth the solver runs on the subdivided mesh rather than the cage: same result, 217 s instead of 8.

Outfits

Outfit builds several garments at once, each on its own layer, worn from the inside out.

  • Casual — tank, trousers, jacket
  • Streetwear — t‑shirt, trousers, hoodie
  • Dress & Jacket
  • Full Layers — tank, t‑shirt, trousers, jacket
  • Workwear — t‑shirt, jumpsuit

Ease is set per layer so each garment clears the one beneath it. Turn on Sew Them to stitch the whole stack in one go.

Getting a slimmer drape

Four fabrics ship as presets, each setting the stiffness values underneath. Crisp / Tailored is the default.

FabricBendingCompressionTake InCharacter
Crisp / Tailored251200.05Holds its shape, few folds
Soft / Jersey0.5150.00Clings, many fine folds
Stiff / Denim602000.03Very firm, broad folds
Light / Silk0.1580.00Fluid, lots of movement

The three levers, in order of effect

  • Bending decides how many folds form at all. Raising it from 0.5 to 25 is most of the difference between crushed and tailored.
  • Take In shrinks the fabric onto the body after the seams are welded, pulling the garment from 13 mm off the skin to under 10 mm. Applying it earlier would fight the stitching, so it waits for the weld.
  • Ease is how much wider than the body the pattern is drafted. Less ease alone does not smooth a garment — the surplus simply buckles harder against the body. Pair it with bending.
Watch the sign. Blender’s shrink is positive‑tightens. A negative value expands the cloth and makes the garment baggier, which is the opposite of what the name suggests.

The grab tool

Pull the cloth by hand. Press Grab Fabric, then drag on the garment to pull it while the simulation keeps running. Release to let go, scroll to resize the grab radius, Esc to finish.

The patch under the cursor is pinned with a soft falloff, so the centre follows your hand and the surrounding cloth trails behind it. Measured on a tank top: with the hand moved 136 mm, the pinned centre travels 109 mm and the rest of the garment shifts 26 mm. Letting go leaves the new shape in place and relaxes it by about 26 mm.

Why it uses a hook. The obvious approach — writing the pin targets straight into the mesh — does nothing: editing mesh data mid‑simulation invalidates the point cache and the solver stops advancing. Driving a Hook modifier placed before the cloth modifier deforms the solver’s input instead, which it follows happily. The rest shape is never touched, so the fabric still springs back when released.

Drawing your own

What Auto Sew decides

Given the drawn vest front and its counterpart, Auto Sew found exactly two seams — the two side edges — and nothing else.

It rejects a pair when the body sits between the two edges, which is what separates a real side seam from a front hem that happens to line up with a back hem. That test runs against a torso‑only collision proxy; including the arms would block legitimate side seams on a figure standing with its arms down.

Several garments at once

Layer sets the wearing order. A garment collides with the body and with every garment on a lower layer, so 0 is worn innermost.

Sew stitches, welds and settles the active garment. Unsew does the opposite — it rebuilds the garment from its flat pieces, drops the rig binding and thickness, and puts the stitches back so you can edit the draft and try again. Sew All and Unsew All work through every layer from the inside out.

One-directional on purpose. An outer layer sees the inner ones, never the reverse. Two cloth objects colliding with each other make the depsgraph cyclic, and Blender silently drops the relationship rather than erroring.
Seams belong to a garment, not the scene. Held globally, adding a second garment wiped the first one's stitching and left it impossible to re-sew — which is why only the most recent garment ever seemed to exist.

How it works

Measuring
The body is described as a stack of horizontal cross‑sections, each storing a centre and a radius per angular sector, so a torso reads as the ellipse it really is. Arms, hands, fingers and head are masked out using the rig’s own skin weights. This matters more than it sounds: with finger bones unmasked, a figure standing in an A‑pose measures a 164 cm waist.
Arranging
Flat pieces are mapped onto the body by arc length at each height. Past 95° the panel leaves the body tangentially instead of winding onto the opposite side. Above the shoulder joint the section is held at its shoulder size — otherwise it collapses to neck radius and a collar would wrap around the throat.
Sewing
A seam becomes a set of loose edges in the cloth mesh, which is what Blender’s solver treats as sewing springs. Stitch direction is taken from the pattern outline, not from distance: a sleeve cap sits 12 cm from its armhole, and picking the direction by proximity is a coin‑toss that shreds one sleeve and not the other.
Draping
Three phases. Stitch at low gravity so the seams close without the garment sliding; weld the paired vertices into one continuous surface; settle at full gravity. The weld is the step that matters — sewing springs never stop pulling, and leaving them on for the whole simulation crushes the fabric.
Finalizing
The draped shape is frozen into the mesh, thickness added, skin weights transferred from the body by nearest‑polygon interpolation, and an Armature modifier bound ahead of the thickness. The finished garment follows the animation.
Why welding matters. Left to run with sewing springs active, the t‑shirt drapes at a mean fold angle of 44° — visibly crushed. Welding mid‑simulation and settling as one piece brings it to 21.6°.

Limits & known behaviour

  • Garments on the same layer do not collide with each other. Collision runs one way only, outer onto inner, so two garments sharing a layer pass through one another. Put them on different layers.
  • Trousers are still the loosest preset, though far closer than they were. Lower the Ease or raise Take In for a slimmer leg.
  • The crisp defaults cost time. Quality 12 and 50 settle frames roughly double simulation time — 14–26 s a garment instead of 5–12 s.
  • A Flat Panel falls to the floor. It has no seams and nothing holds it. That is correct — it is a piece of cloth, not a garment.
  • Draw Pattern is interactive only. It is a modal tool and cannot run headless.
  • Sleeves gather on a character whose arms hang against the ribs, because the sleeve tube starts inside the torso. On the bundled avatar they come out clean.
  • Workspaces live inside each .blend file. The tab is added to files as you open them, and becomes permanent in a file once you save it.

Per‑piece arrangement

Select a pattern piece to get these in the Arrangement panel. With Live Sync on, each one re‑arranges the garment as you drag it.

SettingMeaning
AnchorWhere the piece wraps: torso front/back/left/right, hip, arm or leg
HeightOn the torso, 0 = floor and 1 = top of head. On a limb, the fraction of the way down it
SpinRotates the piece around the body or limb axis
Wrap0 = flat plate, 1 = wrapped around the body
EaseHow far the piece is held off the body surface
ShiftExtra world‑space offset

Installing elsewhere

Already installed and enabled at ~/.config/blender/5.2/scripts/addons/clothing_design.

To install on another machine: Edit › Preferences › Add-ons › Install…, choose clothing_design.zip, then tick Clothing Design. The workspace tab appears on the next file you open; turn that off under the add-on’s preferences if you would rather add it by hand.

Tested on Blender 5.2 LTS, EEVEE renders, RTX 4090. All figures in this page are renders from a single scripted session against the bundled avatar.
